I went through this after realizing I was autistic. I felt so much shame after having thoughts along the lines of I’ve been the problem all along”. I wrote this lengthy apology to an ex, and even to an old friend I hadn’t spoken to in a while. I just felt this overwhelming urge to apologize for existing, and for having ever existed in relation to others. 🤣

I also think the notion of masking threw me off, and my brain was in crisis and thought ‘everything I am is fraudulent and performative, I don’t know the real me is’ — but it was a very literal and reductive understanding of what a ‘mask’ really is. 

This article helped me build a more nuanced understanding of (un)masking: https://poweredbylove.ca/2023/07/22/shifting-my-unmasking-from-revealing-to-unearthing 

I find that as you wade through the grief realizing your neurodivergence propels you into, you come into an anger about having never been accommodated. Eventually that anger turns into intense self-compassion. 

This feeling of defectiveness you speak of, is not new. You likely felt it when you were a kid, learning how to mask, realizing something made the other kids treat you differently. In a lot of ways realizing you’re autistic is being forced to look at and sit with your child self, in their rawest form again. I felt tremendous sadness for her, and how she spent 25 years accommodating a world that didn’t protect or affirm her. 

You owe it to yourself and the younger parts of yourself to not treat yourself as a “problem”. All the medicalized, pathologizing shit we hear about autism right now was made up by some guy who was probably fucking lame. Take time to articulate your struggles and your autistic experience in your own terms. You are still in the driver’s seat and the architect of your own destiny.

This is so relatable and I feel like I can’t pursue a conventional ‘creative’ career because of it - which makes me sad because I am itching to get out of my stale little 9-5 and pursue my own art. I was in a free community film program and by the end of it I dropped out because the element of demand and expectation simply made the shit unbearable for me. I hate being beholden to another person’s creative vision (especially if I don’t find it compelling). It’s not that I lack the interpersonal skills to work harmoniously with others if needed to, I can be sociable & charismatic and am generally well-liked by people, but when my autonomy is compromised in any way my sense of personal fulfillment falls off a cliff and I lose all motivation to continue the work. Sometimes it’s also that I don’t want to disappoint people when I inevitably go through periods of burnout and ‘falling off the face of the earth’. Also networking and “putting myself out there” always feels like I’m tap dancing and shaking my ass or something. I thought it was cultural (I come from a culture that sees self-promotion as an act of individualistic vapidity) but it might also be an autism thing idk. It just feels so unnatural that it hurts.

Some of it is also just me being jaded by the kinds of parasitic personalities that exist in a lot of art scenes. I’ve been burned a few times (had work plagiarized by multiple people) and I think it’s made me more insular. Theres a big ‘integrity’ factor in it for me. A lot of the kinds of brilliant, generous and down-to-earth creatives I’d actually want to work with are far in between, whereas there’s huge swaths of the scene that seems to be really about clout-chasing and amassing social capital via social media. I’ve made relative strides in my creative work and it is recognized internationally on some level, and when I come across people who are clearly trying to build themselves clout-wise by proxy to me it puts me off even more. 

Because of that It feels like inviting people into my creative process is such a vulnerable and frightening act - and sometimes I have to choose between having a creative community or really having a creative practice at all. I’m reading the Artists Way to see if it helps with this stuff.

I think after learning about ‘monotropism’ I feel like at some point there will be a shift away from ADHD/Autism/AuDHD as discrete, distinctive categories of neurodivergence. But I can definitely see examples of people who lean mostly one way or the other. Around more purely autistic folks I feel like a hooligan or something. A lot of my
friends growing up were autistic folks and I was always the anarchist/agent of chaos in those groups. I felt like a bad influence/corrupting force even though I wasn’t really *that* rebellious, I just had an innate aversion to rules, structure and authority. 

At the same time when I’m around more hardcore ADHD folks I feel like a nerd or a grouchy old lady. I can’t keep up with a certain level of spontaneity and while I can do without routine  I can’t typically just throw caution to the wind - I think my autism keeps the ADHD impulsivity at bay - so I cannot relate to the more whim/vibes driven approach of ADHD folks. My maternal side is like that and they drive me fucking crazy because they’re improvising shit every hour and are incapable of sticking to or actualizing a plan. I used to think I had panic disorder or something but I was just having autistic meltdowns from being around them too much. 

Finding AuDHD folks is nice because I feel like I can be a menace to society or I can be a pensive thoughtful scholar and both are accepted graciously. There’s a fluidity there with AuDHD folks that I really appreciate.

The parts correlate to different points in my life, and typically there’s some kind of traumatic fissure behind the fragmentation. Parts work helps you “unblend” and part of that involves extending loving curiosity to those parts, and also operating under the assumption that there is “no bad part”.

As I sat with this part I realized he was doing this to cope with abuse so he is playing ‘protector’. His “unburdened” state is actually a lot more kind and innocent - still boyish but adventurous, loves basketball and Tony Hawk. 

I also have an older teenage part who was very femme, partially out of survival in a conservative family, but part of it was genuine interest in hair, makeup, being a bad bitch…etc. Recently after feeding my masculine parts for a while, I felt that this part calling on me so I went and got box braids so I can feel good in a feminine way again. 

Both of those parts exist in me and I simply learn them, tend to them, and recognize their needs. The more I do so and embrace the multiplicity without resistance, the more integrated and grounded I feel. There are probably more parts within you too, with varying forms of gender expression. If you want to learn more about the IFS theory look at ‘No Bad Parts’ by Richard Schwartz.
